title: Drizzle stitch
subtitle: Cast-on loops coiled onto a stationary needle form dimensional tendrils and stamens
excerpt: Drizzle stitch builds a raised, freestanding tendril or stamen by casting loops onto a needle that is held stationary in the fabric. The loops are slid on one by one, then the needle is drawn through them all to leave a coiled stalk standing above the fabric surface. It is a contemporary stumpwork technique requiring a milliner's needle with a uniform shaft.
sourceNotes: Modern stumpwork tradition; technique widely documented in Jane Nicholas, Stumpwork Embroidery (1995 and subsequent editions) and Di van Niekerk, dimensional embroidery publications. The cast-on loop action is analogous to a knitting cast-on applied to an embroidery needle. FLAG: This is a contemporary technique not present in Dillmont (1886) or Caulfeild and Saward (1882); PUBLIC_DOMAIN is used here in the broad sense of widely disseminated modern technique rather than a dated text.

content.text: Drizzle stitch works by parking a needle in the fabric and then loading it with cast-on loops before pulling through. The needle goes into the fabric and stays there, point down, while the working thread is cast onto it one loop at a time using a motion borrowed from knitting. When enough loops are loaded, the needle is drawn through them and through the fabric in one slow pull. The loops coil together into a raised, dimensional stalk on the surface.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 1 to 2 strands for fine stamens; perle 12 for slightly bolder tendrils

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Tightly woven cotton or linen mounted very firmly in the hoop; the needle must stay vertical without the fabric buckling

items.label: Needle
items.value: Milliner's needle size 3 to 5; the uniform shaft from tip to eye is essential so the loops slide off without catching

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm embroidery hoop; drum-tight tension keeps the needle stable during casting

content.text: Secure the thread on the back and bring it up at (A). Insert the needle back down at (B), very close to (A), perhaps 1 mm away. Do not pull the needle through. Leave it parked vertically in the fabric with the eye and most of the shaft visible above the surface.
Hold the needle steady with your non-dominant hand. Bring the working thread up beside the needle. Wrap the thread over your left thumb to form a small loop.

Slide this loop off your thumb and onto the needle, feeding it from the tip toward the eye. Pull the thread gently so the loop snugs down against the fabric at the base of the needle. This is your first cast-on loop.

Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have the number of loops needed. Six to eight loops make a short stamen. Twelve to fifteen make a longer, curling tendril. Each loop should sit snugly against the one below it, not loose or widely spaced.

Rest the fingers of your non-dominant hand lightly over the loops to hold them together without gripping them tightly. With your dominant hand, take hold of the thread below the fabric and pull the needle slowly and steadily downward through the loops and through the fabric.

As the needle comes through, the coil will form on the surface. Guide it upright with your fingers. Pull the thread firmly enough to seat the base of the coil at (B), but stop before the coil is dragged flat.
Take the thread to the back and secure it. The tendril or stamen now stands free of the fabric surface. A gentle nudge with a needle tip can straighten or curve it slightly.

items.symptom: The loops bunch up or fall off the needle before the pull-through
items.cause: The loops were too loose on the shaft, or the needle was tilted and the loops slipped over the eye end.
items.fix: Keep the needle as vertical as possible throughout. Snug each loop down as you cast it on. A milliner's needle is important here because the eye is the same width as the shaft; a tapestry or embroidery needle widens at the eye and the loops will catch.

items.symptom: The coil collapses flat when the needle is pulled through
items.cause: The thread was pulled too fast or too hard, or the loops were not held together during the pull.
items.fix: Rest a finger over the loops before pulling. Pull slowly and steadily, watching the coil form. Stop as soon as the base reaches the fabric; do not continue pulling.

items.symptom: The base of the tendril looks loose or gappy at the fabric surface
items.cause: The entry point (A) and exit point (B) were too far apart, leaving a visible gap at the root.
items.fix: Keep (A) and (B) no more than 1 to 2 mm apart. The tendril should rise from a single point.
